chapters.title: The Habit Loop
chapters.keys: This week, pick one habit you want to change and write down its three parts. Duhigg's habit loop is a cue, the trigger that tells the brain to go on autopilot and which habit to run, then a routine, the behavior itself, then a reward, which tells the brain the loop is worth keeping. Chunking is his word for the brain turning a chain of actions into one automatic routine, work done in an old, deep part of the brain called the basal ganglia. He says this happens because the brain is always looking for ways to save effort, so once a habit forms, the thinking part of the brain stops fully taking part in the decision. That is why, he says, a habit runs on its own unless you deliberately fight it or find a new routine. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Eugene Pauly, known as EP, had his memory destroyed by a brain infection, yet he learned to walk around his block every day and come home, and to find the kitchen, while being unable to say where he lived; the scientist Larry Squire studied him to show that habits live apart from memory. The chapter also reports MIT experiments in which rats learning a maze showed less and less brain activity as the run became a habit.

chapters.title: The Craving Brain
chapters.keys: To build a new habit, choose a simple, obvious cue and a clear reward, then let yourself come to crave that reward. Craving is Duhigg's name for the anticipation of the reward that sets in as soon as the cue appears, and he says it is what powers the habit loop. The cue and reward alone are not enough; a habit takes hold once the brain starts expecting the reward and longing for it. He reports Wolfram Schultz's study of a monkey named Julio, whose brain began reacting to the cue before the juice arrived and who became frustrated when the juice did not come. He says people who stick with exercise do the same thing: they pick a specific cue and a specific reward and come to crave it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Claude Hopkins sold Pepsodent by pointing people to the film on their teeth as a cue, and the paste contained ingredients that made the mouth tingle, a feeling people came to crave, and it became a huge seller. Procter & Gamble's Febreze flopped at first because people living with bad smells could not notice them, but after researchers watched people clean, it was relaunched with a scent as the finishing touch at the end of cleaning, and sales took off.

chapters.title: The Golden Rule of Habit Change
chapters.keys: You cannot wipe out a bad habit, only change it, so keep the old cue, keep the old reward, and swap in a new routine. Duhigg calls this the golden rule of habit change. Habit reversal training is his example of the method in practice: first awareness training, where you write down each time the cue strikes, then a competing response, a new behavior you do instead when it does. He adds a second ingredient, belief: for the change to last under stress, people must believe they can change, and that belief most often comes from being part of a group. He says Alcoholics Anonymous works this way: it keeps drinkers' cues and rewards such as relief and companionship but replaces drinking with meetings and a sponsor, and the group makes belief possible. Reversal: Duhigg says the golden rule alone often breaks down in moments of high stress, when people fall back on old routines unless belief is added. Story the author tells: Coach Tony Dungy built the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on a few simple plays the players ran by habit, and the team got good but kept collapsing in big playoff games when players slid back to old habits. A woman named Mandy stopped biting her nails by noting her cue and doing a competing response. Later, at the Indianapolis Colts, after the death of Dungy's son, the players came to believe, and the Colts won the Super Bowl.

chapters.title: Keystone Habits, or The Ballad of Paul O'Neill
chapters.keys: Find one keystone habit and put your effort there. Keystone habits are Duhigg's name for habits that matter more than others because changing them sets off a chain reaction that reshapes other habits. Small wins are his name for small advantages that build momentum and convince people bigger changes are possible. Keystone habits also work, he says, by creating structures and cultures that let other changes take hold. He reports a study in which people asked to keep a food journal lost more weight, because the journal led to other changes in how they planned and ate. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Paul O'Neill took over Alcoa and announced that his priority would be worker safety, with any injury reported to him within a day along with a plan to stop it happening again; this forced lines of communication from the factory floor to the top that changed how the whole company ran, and Alcoa's profits hit records. Michael Phelps's coach, Bob Bowman, gave Phelps routines such as mentally playing a videotape of a perfect race, and when Phelps's goggles filled with water at the Beijing Olympics, Phelps swam by counting strokes and won gold with a world record.

chapters.title: Starbucks and the Habit of Success
chapters.keys: Treat willpower as a habit you build by deciding ahead of time what you will do at hard moments. Duhigg calls willpower the single most important keystone habit for individual success. He reports that willpower works like a muscle that tires with use, as in the study where people told to eat radishes and not touch nearby cookies gave up faster on a later puzzle. Inflection points are his name for the moments of pain or temptation where willpower fails, and the move is to write down a plan for each one in advance. Starbucks teaches employees routines for these moments, such as the LATTE method for an angry customer: Listen, Acknowledge the complaint, Take action, Thank them, Explain why it happened. He also reports that people given a sense of control, such as being asked politely and given a reason, used less willpower doing what was asked. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Travis Leach grew up with parents addicted to drugs and kept losing jobs when he lost his temper, until Starbucks training taught him willpower routines, and he became a store manager. The chapter also reports a Scottish hospital study where elderly hip and knee surgery patients who wrote plans for the painful moments of recovery started walking faster.

chapters.title: The Power of a Crisis
chapters.keys: Leaders should use a crisis, or create a sense of one, to remake the habits of an organization. Duhigg says every company has organizational habits, which he calls routines, unwritten patterns that let work get done without constant decisions. Those routines also create truces, informal deals between rival groups that keep the peace, and he warns that a truce can be dangerous when it lets problems go unaddressed. He says organizational habits become open to change during a crisis, so good leaders seize the moment and some even stretch it out. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: at Rhode Island Hospital, a truce in which nurses deferred to surgeons led to a surgeon operating on the wrong side of a patient's head, and the patient died; after more errors, the hospital overhauled its safety routines. In London's King's Cross station, a fire started under an escalator, where rubbish had built up, and killed dozens, because separate departments each assumed safety was someone else's job; the investigator Desmond Fennell found no one was responsible and his report changed the rules.

chapters.title: How Target Knows What You Want Before You Do
chapters.keys: If you want people to take up something new, dress it in something they already know. Duhigg says habits are most open to change at big life events such as having a baby, and companies like Target use data to spot those moments and win new shopping habits. He says people resist things that feel unfamiliar, even when they like them, so a new product has to be mixed in with familiar things before it is accepted. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Target statistician Andrew Pole built a model to spot pregnant customers from their purchases; an angry father near Minneapolis complained that Target was sending baby coupons to his teenage daughter and later apologized because she was pregnant, and Target learned to hide baby ads among unrelated items such as lawn mowers.

chapters.title: Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott
chapters.keys: Duhigg says a movement grows through a three-part process: it starts from the habits of friendship and strong ties among close acquaintances, it spreads through the habits of a community and its weak ties, people who know each other a little and feel social pressure to join, and it lasts because a leader gives people new habits and a new sense of who they are, so the movement can run on its own. He says weak ties matter because they reach far beyond one circle, and he reports that people looking for jobs found them more often through acquaintances than close friends. He reports a study of Freedom Summer volunteers, where people with ties to church and community groups who had signed up were the ones who actually went. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery in 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat; she had strong friendships across the city's social groups, so her friends rallied to her, and weak ties drew the wider Black community into a bus boycott.

chapters.title: The Neurology of Free Will
chapters.keys: Once you know a habit exists, you are responsible for changing it. Duhigg says habits are not destiny, and the person who sees the cue, routine and reward of a habit has the power to change it. He says belief that you can change is what makes change possible, as the philosopher William James held. Reversal: Duhigg says a person acting with no awareness of the habit, as in sleep, is not responsible in the same way as someone who knows the habit and can choose to change it. Story the author tells: Angie Bachmann, a stay-at-home mother, gambled away her inheritance and her home; when the casino company went after her for her unpaid debts she countersued, saying it had exploited her habit, and she lost; Duhigg says she knew about her habit and so was responsible.
